questions.prompt: Where does a sync engine mutator run?

options.label: Only on the client; the server validates the resulting state
Only on the server; the client reads back the result
Twice — optimistically on the client and authoritatively on the server
Inside the database as a stored procedure

questions.explanation: The mutator is shared code: it runs locally the instant the user triggers it (optimistic UI), and again on the server when the client pushes the queued mutation (authoritative state). That dual-run requirement is why mutators must be deterministic — no Date.now(), no random IDs inside the body.

questions.prompt: What's the shape of Replicache's client-side store?

options.label: Key-value, scanned by prefix, persisted to IndexedDB
Relational tables queried with SQL
An append-only event log
An in-memory normalized graph, no persistence

questions.explanation: Replicache is a KV store. You read with tx.get and tx.scan({ prefix }), write with tx.set and tx.del. Persistence lives in IndexedDB. Zero's model is closer to (b); LiveStore is (a) and (c) combined (SQLite materialized from events).

questions.prompt: What technology backs LiveStore's local store?

options.label: IndexedDB with a typed wrapper
localStorage + a CRDT library
SQLite compiled to WebAssembly, persisted via OPFS/IndexedDB
DuckDB via the Arrow web bindings

questions.explanation: LiveStore runs a WASM build of SQLite in the browser and persists it through OPFS (or IndexedDB as a fallback). That's what gives it real SQL — joins, indexes, aggregates — on tens of thousands of rows. Events are the source of truth; the SQLite tables are a materialized view derived by materializers.

questions.prompt: Why does a sync engine beat Tanstack Query + WebSocket for collaborative apps?

options.label: Sync engines are faster because they use HTTP/3
They have a mutator + reconciliation model (replay, rebase, deterministic writes), not just a request/response cache
Tanstack Query doesn't support real-time updates at all
Sync engines avoid the network entirely on every interaction

questions.explanation: Tanstack Query is a cache of server responses; mutations are opaque calls that invalidate keys. A sync engine adds typed mutators that run on both sides, a pending-mutation queue, and a rebase loop that reapplies pending writes on top of server diffs. That model — not the transport — is what makes offline replay and multi-tab consistency work.

questions.prompt: Which domain is the WORST fit for a sync engine?

options.label: Collaborative issue tracker (multiple users editing the same issue)
Banking app where the server must definitively accept or reject every transaction before it's considered done
Real-time multiplayer whiteboard
Email client with offline reading and queued sends

questions.explanation: Sync engines are optimistic by default — the client commits the write locally, then reconciles. For server-of-truth domains like banking, payments, or anything regulated, that semantic is a liability: a transfer can't appear true to the user if the server is going to reject it. Use a conventional API with explicit pending states. The other options are exactly what sync engines are for.
